title: Signal-Transduction Pathways: How Cells Compute With Molecular Switches

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: List, in order, the five components of a membrane-receptor signaling pathway.
cards.back: First messenger (outside) → receptor → second messenger (inside) → effector molecules → physiological response.
cards.quote: a primary (first) messenger arrives from outside, binds a receptor, which generates or activates a second messenger inside the cell,
cards.section: The parts: messengers, receptors, effectors

cards.front: Beyond its five components, a membrane-receptor pathway needs a sixth feature, {{c1::active termination}}: the pathway has to be switched off on purpose.
cards.quote: A sixth feature is easy to forget: active termination; the pathway has to be switched off on purpose.
cards.section: The parts: messengers, receptors, effectors

cards.front: Why do steroid hormones have receptors inside the cell, while peptide hormones and growth factors use receptors that span the plasma membrane?
cards.back: Small, lipophilic signals cross the membrane and find internal receptors. Large or polar signals cannot cross, so a membrane-spanning receptor must read them outside.
cards.quote: Large or polar signals, such as peptide hormones and growth factors, cannot cross, so they must be read by a receptor that spans the membrane.
cards.section: The parts: messengers, receptors, effectors

cards.front: Name five second messengers.
cards.back: cAMP, IP3, DAG, calcium (Ca²⁺) and PIP3.
cards.why: A second messenger is made or released inside the cell after the receptor fires.
cards.quote: A second messenger is made or released after the receptor fires and relays the order inside the cell: cAMP, IP3, DAG, calcium, PIP3.
cards.section: The parts: messengers, receptors, effectors

cards.front: How does an activated GPCR switch on its heterotrimeric G protein, and what is the receptor's role called?
cards.back: It pries GDP off the alpha subunit and lets GTP take its place. That makes the receptor alpha's GEF (guanine-nucleotide exchange factor): it pushes the switch ON.
cards.quote: That makes the receptor alpha's GEF (guanine-nucleotide exchange factor): it pushes the switch ON.
cards.section: One switch first: the G-protein cycle

cards.front: What switches an active G-alpha subunit back off?
cards.back: Its own GTPase activity slowly hydrolyzes GTP to GDP, a built-in timer. Alpha-GDP then rejoins beta-gamma and goes quiet.
cards.quote: Alpha is itself a GTPase, an enzyme that slowly cuts its own GTP back to GDP: a built-in timer.
cards.section: One switch first: the G-protein cycle

cards.front: What does each G-alpha type do: Gs, Gi and Gq?
cards.back: Gs stimulates adenylate cyclase (cAMP up). Gi inhibits adenylate cyclase (cAMP down). Gq activates phospholipase C, launching the calcium branch.
cards.quote: Gs stimulates adenylate cyclase and raises cAMP. Gi inhibits it and lowers cAMP.
cards.section: One switch first: the G-protein cycle

cards.front: Epinephrine reaches two cells: one expresses a Gs-coupled receptor, the other a Gi-coupled receptor. Predict cAMP in each, and state the principle.
cards.back: cAMP rises in the Gs cell and falls in the Gi cell. The response is written into the receptor, its G protein and the cell's machinery, not into the ligand.
cards.quote: because the response is written into the receptor, its G protein and the machinery of that cell, not into the ligand.
cards.section: One switch first: the G-protein cycle

cards.front: In broken liver cells, adrenaline worked only if the membrane fraction was present, yet the factor that switched on phosphorylase appeared in the soluble fraction. What did this show?
cards.back: The membrane converts the hormone's arrival into a small, water-soluble internal messenger: cyclic AMP, the first second messenger identified.
cards.quote: Adrenaline needed the membrane fraction of broken liver cells to work, yet the factor that switched on phosphorylase appeared in the soluble fraction.
cards.section: The cAMP relay: a chain of switches

cards.front: Which enzyme makes cAMP, from what, and which enzyme degrades it?
cards.back: Adenylate cyclase makes cAMP from ATP (clipping off two phosphates and cyclizing the rest). Phosphodiesterase (PDE) converts cAMP to AMP.
cards.quote: Adenylate cyclase makes cAMP from ATP by clipping off two phosphates and cyclizing the rest.
cards.section: The cAMP relay: a chain of switches

cards.front: How does cAMP activate protein kinase A (PKA)?
cards.back: PKA rests as an R2C2 tetramer, with two regulatory subunits clamping two catalytic subunits silent. cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, they let go, and the catalytic subunits come free and active.
cards.quote: cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, they let go, and the catalytic subunits come free and active.
cards.section: The cAMP relay: a chain of switches

cards.front: A compound frees PKA's catalytic subunits in liver cells with no hormone present. Predict the effect on glycogen phosphorylase, glycogen synthase and net glycogen.
cards.back: Phosphorylase is switched on (via phosphorylase kinase) and glycogen synthase is switched off, so glycogen is broken down and not rebuilt.
cards.why: PKA uses both signs of phosphorylation at once: activating breakdown, inhibiting synthesis.
cards.quote: It switches on breakdown (phosphorylase kinase, then phosphorylase) and switches off synthesis (glycogen synthase), so stored glucose is released and not rebuilt.
cards.section: The cAMP relay: a chain of switches

cards.front: In a membrane-receptor signaling pathway, what sets how much of any one switch is ON at a given moment?
cards.back: The contest between its ON reaction and its OFF reaction. Every switch is pushed ON by one reaction and pulled OFF by another.
cards.quote: Every switch in a pathway is pushed ON by one reaction and pulled OFF by another,
cards.section: The cAMP relay: a chain of switches

cards.front: What are the two ways a signaling switch can become stuck ON?
cards.back: It loses its OFF reaction, or it stops needing its ON signal.
cards.quote: a switch sticks ON when it loses its OFF reaction or stops needing its ON signal.
cards.section: The cAMP relay: a chain of switches

cards.front: For an enzyme step in a signaling relay, gain = how fast the active form works × {{c1::how long it stays active}}.
cards.back: The step's OFF reaction sets that lifetime.
cards.quote: gain = how fast the active form works × how long it stays active
cards.section: How big: speed times lifetime, multiplied down the chain

cards.front: In round teaching numbers, an adenylate cyclase makes about 10 cAMP per second while its Gs-alpha stays ON for about 10 seconds. How many cAMP does it make? If a slower GTPase kept Gs-alpha ON for 30 seconds, how many?
cards.back: Gain = rate × lifetime: 10 cAMP/s × 10 s = about 100 cAMP. With 30 s ON: 10 × 30 = about 300 cAMP. The OFF arm sets the gain.
cards.quote: a cyclase making about 10 cAMP a second, switched on by a Gs-alpha that stays ON for about 10 seconds, makes about 100 cAMP.
cards.section: How big: speed times lifetime, multiplied down the chain

cards.front: Teaching gains for the beta-adrenergic relay: receptor→Gs ×10; Gs→cyclase ×1; cyclase→cAMP ×100; cAMP→PKA ×½; PKA→phosphorylase kinase ×10; phosphorylase kinase→phosphorylase ×10; phosphorylase→glucose 1-phosphate ×1,000. How many glucose units per epinephrine molecule, and why are two steps ×1 and ×½?
cards.back: 10 × 1 × 100 × ½ × 10 × 10 × 1,000 = 50,000,000. The ×1 and ×½ steps are binding steps, not enzymes: one Gs-alpha binds one cyclase; four cAMP free two catalytic subunits.
cards.section: How big: speed times lifetime, multiplied down the chain

cards.front: Starting from the 50 million glucose units of the beta-adrenergic teaching relay, a mutation halves the PKA→phosphorylase kinase gain from 10 to 5. What is the new output? If the seven gains (10, 1, 100, ½, 10, 10, 1,000) added instead of multiplying, how much would the same change matter?
cards.back: Multiplied: 50,000,000 × 5/10 = 25,000,000, a halving. Added: 1,131.5 falls to 1,126.5, barely moving. Halving any one factor halves a product, which is why single steps are where toxins, mutations and drugs act.
cards.quote: (a) It doubles, to 100 million: doubling any one factor doubles a product.
cards.section: How big: speed times lifetime, multiplied down the chain

cards.front: Epinephrine is already high enough that every downstream phosphorylase is ON. The dose is doubled. Predict glucose output and explain.
cards.back: Output barely rises. The product rule holds only while each step has spare enzyme to switch on; once a step's enzyme is all ON, output hits a ceiling set by whichever step runs out first.
cards.quote: Push in a big enough signal and the downstream enzyme is all ON already, so the output stops rising.
cards.section: How big: speed times lifetime, multiplied down the chain

cards.front: What happens to a signaling switch when its OFF arm is weakened?
cards.back: Its steady level rises, just as if the ON arm had been strengthened, and it also takes longer to switch off.
cards.quote: Weaken it and that switch's steady level rises, just as if you had strengthened the ON arm, though it now also takes longer to switch off.
cards.section: How long: the slowest OFF step

cards.front: In a simple model of the relay, liver cells exposed to epinephrine are given a high dose of a phosphodiesterase inhibitor. Predict the cAMP level, and whether cAMP persists much longer after the hormone is washed out.
cards.back: cAMP rises, but lasts only a little longer after washout. Cyclase keeps making cAMP until Gs-alpha switches off, and in a simple model the G protein is the slowest OFF step on the way to cAMP. Bigger, not longer.
cards.quote: So blocking PDE mostly makes cAMP bigger, not longer.
cards.section: How long: the slowest OFF step

cards.front: How does cholera toxin act on Gs-alpha, and what follows in intestinal cells?
cards.back: It ADP-ribosylates Gs-alpha so it can no longer hydrolyze GTP. Gs is locked ON, cAMP never stops, and chloride and water pour into the intestine.
cards.quote: In cholera, choleragen chemically modifies Gs-alpha by ADP-ribosylation (attaching an ADP-ribose group) so it can no longer hydrolyze its GTP.
cards.section: Broken switches: four ways to break the contest

cards.front: An intestinal cell exposed to cholera toxin is also given a drug that raises phosphodiesterase activity. Predict the effect on cAMP, and whether this restores normal shut-off.
cards.back: cAMP falls somewhat, because strengthening cAMP's OFF arm lowers its steady level. It does not restore shut-off: Gs is still locked ON, so cyclase keeps making cAMP.
cards.why: Rests on the contest rule: each switch's level is set by its own ON and OFF arms.
cards.quote: Gs is locked ON, cAMP never stops, and chloride and water pour into the intestine.
cards.section: Broken switches: four ways to break the contest

cards.front: A toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi so it cannot be switched ON. Predict cAMP in the target cell, and explain why a G protein stuck OFF does not mean less signal.
cards.back: cAMP goes up. Gi normally holds adenylate cyclase back; stuck OFF, it is a brake that can no longer lower cAMP. This is pertussis toxin.
cards.quote: sounds like less signal, but Gi is a brake that can no longer lower cAMP.
cards.section: Broken switches: four ways to break the contest

cards.front: In some cases of Cushing's syndrome, how is the PKA switch broken?
cards.back: A mutation leaves PKA's catalytic subunit unable to bind its regulatory subunit, so PKA escapes its clamp and cortisol production runs with no hormone signal. The switch is freed from its ON signal.
cards.quote: In some cases of Cushing's syndrome, a mutation leaves PKA's catalytic subunit unable to bind its regulatory subunit.
cards.section: Broken switches: four ways to break the contest

cards.front: In a Cushing's tumor whose PKA catalytic subunit cannot bind its regulatory subunit, would a drug that boosts phosphodiesterase activity lower cortisol output? Why or why not?
cards.back: Little or no effect. Lowering cAMP acts on the ON signal, but this PKA no longer needs cAMP; its activity is set downstream of the step the drug targets.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that a switch freed from its ON signal is ON with no signal at all.
cards.quote: Nothing is wrong with PDE or the phosphatases here; the switch simply no longer needs cAMP.
cards.section: Broken switches: four ways to break the contest

cards.front: When Gq activates phospholipase C, what are the two products of PIP2 cleavage and what does each do?
cards.back: IP3 is soluble and opens IP3-gated Ca²⁺ channels on the endoplasmic reticulum. DAG stays in the membrane and, with that Ca²⁺, activates protein kinase C.
cards.why: Conventional PKC needs both signals, so it is a coincidence detector.
cards.quote: IP3 is soluble; it floats to the endoplasmic reticulum and opens an IP3-gated calcium channel, releasing a flood of Ca²⁺.
cards.section: The Gq branch: one cut, two messengers

cards.front: The common reader of the Ca²⁺ second messenger is {{c1::calmodulin}}, which carries four Ca²⁺-binding EF-hand motifs.
cards.back: Each EF hand is a helix-loop-helix fold.
cards.quote: Calcium is a ubiquitous second messenger, and its common reader is calmodulin, which carries four Ca²⁺-binding EF-hand motifs, each a helix-loop-helix fold.
cards.section: The Gq branch: one cut, two messengers

cards.front: Which two pumps form the OFF arm of a cytosolic Ca²⁺ signal, and where does each send calcium?
cards.back: PMCA pumps Ca²⁺ out of the cell; SERCA returns it to the endoplasmic reticulum.
cards.quote: the PMCA pushes calcium out of the cell, and the SERCA pump returns it to the endoplasmic reticulum.
cards.section: The Gq branch: one cut, two messengers

cards.front: Outline growth hormone signaling through JAK-STAT, from binding to gene expression.
cards.back: Growth hormone binds a pre-assembled receptor pair; the two attached JAK2s cross-phosphorylate, then phosphorylate the receptor tails. STAT5 docks, is phosphorylated, dimerizes and enters the nucleus to change gene expression.
cards.quote: Binding moves the two JAK2s into position, and they phosphorylate each other (cross-phosphorylation), then the receptor tails.
cards.section: Receptors that recruit a kinase: JAK-STAT

cards.front: Trace EGFR signaling to Ras activation, and name Ras's ON and OFF arms.
cards.back: EGF binding dimerizes EGFR, the halves cross-phosphorylate, and phospho-tyrosines dock Grb2, which brings SOS. SOS (Ras's GEF) loads GTP: ON. Ras's own GTPase, sped up by GAPs: OFF.
cards.why: Active Ras drives the Raf-MEK-ERK cascade toward proliferation.
cards.quote: SOS is Ras's GEF: it pushes Ras ON.
cards.section: Receptors that are kinases: EGFR and Ras

cards.front: Compare oncogenic Ras (GAP-assisted GTPase blocked) with the Cushing's PKA mutant (catalytic subunit cannot bind its regulatory subunit). Which still needs its ON signal, and which earlier switch does each resemble?
cards.back: Mutant Ras still needs SOS to load GTP: a lost OFF arm, like Gs-alpha in cholera. Mutant PKA needs no cAMP: freed from its ON signal, like Bcr-Abl.
cards.why: Rests on the two ways a switch sticks ON: losing its OFF reaction, or no longer needing its ON signal.
cards.quote: It is the lost-OFF-arm story again, one tier down.
cards.section: Receptors that are kinases: EGFR and Ras

cards.front: Through which kinase does insulin signaling act to produce glucose uptake, and how does that uptake happen in muscle and fat?
cards.back: Akt drives GLUT4 translocation to the membrane for glucose uptake in muscle and fat. Akt also drives glycogen synthesis in muscle and liver.
cards.quote: Akt drives the two outcomes that define the fed state: GLUT4 translocation to the membrane for glucose uptake in muscle and fat,
cards.section: Insulin: the lipid-kinase deep dive

cards.front: PIP2 is the substrate of both phospholipase C and PI3K. What does each enzyme do to it?
cards.back: PLC cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG. PI3K, a lipid kinase, phosphorylates PIP2 into PIP3. Same substrate, different chemistry, different messengers.
cards.quote: In the Gq branch, PLC cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG. In insulin signaling, PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 into PIP3.
cards.section: Insulin: the lipid-kinase deep dive

cards.front: A tumor cell line lacks PTEN. Predict PIP3 and Akt activity, and name the kind of switch failure.
cards.back: PIP3 builds up and Akt stays active, promoting growth and survival. PTEN is the OFF arm that converts PIP3 back to PIP2, so this is a lost OFF arm; PTEN is a tumor suppressor.
cards.quote: PTEN is a tumor suppressor: lose it, and PIP3 builds up and Akt stays active, which helps drive many cancers.
cards.section: Insulin: the lipid-kinase deep dive

cards.front: A patient's muscle cells have a partial block at IRS. Predict insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, and classify the switch failure.
cards.back: Glucose uptake falls, because less signal reaches PI3K, PIP3, Akt and GLUT4. This is a weakened ON arm (insulin resistance): too little response, not too much.
cards.why: Insulin resistance is one half of type 2 diabetes; the other is beta cells unable to make enough insulin to overcome it.
cards.quote: Weakened signaling along this chain (insulin resistance) is one half of type 2 diabetes;
cards.section: Insulin: the lipid-kinase deep dive

cards.front: Distinguish a proto-oncogene from a tumor-suppressor gene.
cards.back: Proto-oncogenes promote growth and become oncogenes when stuck ON. Tumor-suppressor genes brake growth or guard the genome, and help cause cancer when lost.
cards.quote: Proto-oncogenes promote growth and become oncogenes when stuck ON; tumor-suppressor genes brake growth or guard the genome, and help cause cancer when lost.
cards.section: Drugs on the wiring

cards.front: Contrast how Gleevec (imatinib) and cetuximab block cancer signaling.
cards.back: Gleevec wedges into the ATP-binding pocket of the always-ON Bcr-Abl kinase in CML, acting inside on the stuck switch. Cetuximab is an antibody that blocks EGF binding EGFR outside, preventing dimerization.
cards.quote: Gleevec wedges into the kinase's ATP-binding pocket and shuts it off,
cards.section: Drugs on the wiring

cards.front: Two tumors: one is EGFR-driven with normal KRAS; the other carries a KRAS mutation that keeps Ras GTP-bound. Which is likely to respond to cetuximab, and why?
cards.back: Only the EGFR-driven tumor. In the KRAS tumor the pathway is stuck ON below the receptor; mutant KRAS stays GTP-loaded without EGFR, so blocking the upstream ON arm does little.
cards.quote: Weakening an ON arm upstream does little to a switch that has lost its OFF arm,
cards.section: Drugs on the wiring

cards.front: State the general rule for where a drug should act on a stuck signaling switch, using Gleevec in CML and cetuximab in KRAS-mutant tumors as the two cases.
cards.back: A drug aimed above a switch that is stuck ON usually does little. Gleevec hits Bcr-Abl directly and works; cetuximab acts above stuck Ras and usually fails. Knowing the tumor's genetics shows which step is stuck.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that weakening an upstream ON arm does little to a switch stuck ON below it.
cards.quote: It acts from the inside, on the stuck switch itself.
cards.section: Drugs on the wiring

cards.front: In a three-switch model (G-alpha, cAMP, a phosphorylated target), only the phosphatase is slowed, giving the phosphate a half-life of about 80 seconds. The target's half-time after the hormone leaves stretches to about 90 seconds. What does this show?
cards.back: The response can outlast its second messenger: the final step's own OFF arm, phosphatases undoing phosphorylations, can set the response's duration independently of cAMP.
cards.quote: stretched the target's half-time to about 90 seconds: the response can outlast its second messenger.
cards.section: Size and duration in a model relay

cards.front: In a model relay you want to find which OFF step limits how long cAMP lasts after the hormone leaves. You compare halving PDE with blocking the G-alpha GTPase. What results would show the G protein is the slowest OFF step?
cards.back: Halving PDE lengthens cAMP's half-time only slightly (in the model, about 9 to about 11 seconds), while blocking the GTPase keeps cAMP up after the hormone leaves.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the response dies away at about the pace of its slowest OFF step.
cards.quote: With the GTPase blocked, as in cholera, cAMP stayed up after the hormone left,
cards.section: Size and duration in a model relay

cards.front: GLP-1 receptor agonists act on a Gs-coupled GPCR on pancreatic cells. Predict the second messenger they raise, and explain why these drugs rarely cause hypoglycemia, unlike sulfonylureas.
cards.back: cAMP, via Gs and adenylate cyclase. The insulin boost depends on glucose: strong when blood glucose is high, fading as glucose falls, so insulin release is not driven at low glucose.
cards.why: Combines the Gs logic (cAMP up) with the glucose-dependence built into GLP-1's wiring.
cards.quote: GLP-1 boosts insulin release when blood glucose is high, and the boost fades as glucose falls.
cards.section: GLP-1 drugs

cards.front: For an agonist in a given assay, {{c1::efficacy}} is how large the maximal response can get (Emax); potency is the dose that gives half the maximal response (EC₅₀).
cards.quote: Potency is how much drug it takes to get half the maximal response (the EC₅₀); efficacy is how large that maximal response can get (Emax).
cards.section: Potency and efficacy

cards.front: A competitive antagonist is added to an agonist dose-response experiment. Predict the change in EC₅₀ and in Emax.
cards.back: EC₅₀ rises (the curve shifts right; apparent potency falls) while Emax is unchanged, because enough extra agonist always wins the competition back.
cards.quote: add a competitive antagonist and watch the curve slide right while its ceiling stays put:
cards.section: Potency and efficacy
